title: Quantum side information that cannot be compressed
authors: Lasse H. Wolff, Matthias Christandl, Bergfinnur Durhuus, Christoph Hirche, Andreas Winter
problem: If a small classical variable \(X\) is correlated with a large one \(Y\), then \(Y\) can be compressed, by a channel, to a variable whose size depends only on the size of \(X\) and the allowed error, while keeping almost all of the mutual information with \(X\). Results of this kind bound the auxiliary variables in many optimization formulas of information theory and give a theoretical basis for the information-bottleneck view of learning. Does the same hold when the large system is quantum: can a large system \(B\) correlated with a small system \(A\) be compressed to a size depending on \(A\) alone, losing arbitrarily little mutual information?
result: No. For every nontrivial \(A\) and every sufficiently large \(B\) there are states \(\rho_{AB}\) for which every channel from \(B\) to a smaller system \(C\) loses mutual information at least \(\tfrac14f(|A|)\log e\,(1-|C|/|B|)^2\), where \(f(|A|)>2.4\times10^{-4}\) and \(f\) tends to one as \(|A|\) grows. The loss does not shrink as \(B\) grows, so no compression by a nontrivial fraction is nearly lossless. Random states of a simple form have this property with high probability. Tensor powers raise the loss to \(0.035\log|A|\) for compression to any fixed size, and a random-state construction in the appendix reaches \(2\log|A|-O(\log\log|A|)\), even if an unlimited classical record is kept alongside.
significance: The result marks a clean separation between classical and quantum side information. For formulas such as the quantum information bottleneck, squashed entanglement and conditional entanglement of mutual information, there can be no general dimension bound on the quantum auxiliary system obtained by compression. For quantum machine learning, a small set of relevant features carried by a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact quantum encoding that preserves them. Read the other way, classical features hidden in quantum data can be protected against any learner whose quantum memory is bounded.
limitations: The basic loss bound is small in absolute terms, a few thousandths of a bit for the four-dimensional \(A\) of the main construction, though independent of the size of \(B\). The states come from Haar-random unitaries, and the statements hold with probability tending to one as \(|B|\) grows, with no explicit finite-size rates. Whether compression can be ruled out when \(A\) is a classical bit is open, and there is evidence it may be possible. Compression remains possible when the quantum part of \(B\) in the Koashi–Imoto decomposition is bounded. The authors acknowledge the use of ChatGPT 6.0 Astra in proving Lemma 16, which supplied a missing piece of the tighter random-state argument in Appendix F, and for proofreading, and state that no language model was used for the main theorem or its corollaries.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: The question is posed as compression with a channel \(T\) from \(B\) to \(C\), judged by the mutual information \(I(A:C)\) that survives. Classically one can always reach \(|C|\le(4/\epsilon)^{|X|}\) with loss of order \(\epsilon\log|X|\), by grouping values of \(Y\) whose conditional distributions of \(X\) are close. A similar statement holds when \(B\) is classical and \(A\) quantum. The new result concerns the reverse case, where the system to be compressed is quantum.

The first step converts information loss into a recovery problem. If a channel loses little mutual information, then a recovery channel from \(C\) back to \(B\) restores the joint state with small trace-distance error, by the recovery theorem for approximate quantum Markov chains. Conversely, good recovery implies little information loss by continuity of conditional entropy. So it suffices to construct states for which no pair of channels through a smaller system can restore \(\rho_{AB}\) accurately.

The construction is a random controlled unitary. Pick \(j\) at random among \(K=\lfloor|A|/2\rfloor\) values, put \(A\) in \((\ket{2j-1}+\ket{2j})/\sqrt2\), and apply the unitary \(U_j\) to a maximally mixed \(B\), controlled on which of the two basis states \(A\) is in. The unitaries are Haar random. The state carries one bit of mutual information however large \(B\) is, and that bit is stored in the coherence between \(U_j\) and the identity.

Any compression followed by recovery is a channel on \(B\) whose Kraus operators have rank at most \(|C|\). A witness operator built from the \(U_j\) converts the recovery error into a sum of squared commutators between these Kraus operators and the random unitaries. Random unitaries form a quantum expander, by a theorem of Hastings, so no operator can nearly commute with all of them unless it is close to a multiple of the identity, and a low-rank operator cannot be. This gives a recovery error at least \((1-\sqrt{2K-1}/K-\varepsilon)(1-|C|/|B|)\), and the information bound follows.

methods.technique: From lost mutual information to failed recovery
methods.explanation: Mutual information lost by a channel equals a conditional mutual information in the channel's dilation. Small conditional mutual information means an approximate Markov chain, which can be undone by a recovery map. So incompressibility can be proved by showing that recovery fails.
math: Let \(T:B\to C\) have Stinespring isometry \(B\to CE\). Then \(I(A:B)=I(A:CE)\), and the chain rule gives \[I(A:B)-I(A:C)=I(A:E\,|\,C).\] If this is at most \(\epsilon\), the recovery theorem for approximate Markov chains supplies \(R:C\to B\) with \[\bigl\|\rho_{AB}-(\mathrm{id}_A\otimes R\circ T)(\rho_{AB})\bigr\|_1\le2\sqrt{\epsilon/\log e}.\]

Conversely, if some recovery restores the state to trace distance \(\delta\), the Alicki–Fannes continuity bound for conditional entropy shows that \(T\) loses at most \(\delta\log|A|+g(\delta/2)\), with \(g(x)=(1+x)\log(1+x)-x\log x\). So a lower bound \(F\) on the recovery error for all channel pairs gives the information bound \(\epsilon\ge\tfrac14F^2\log e\), which is the form of Theorem 1.

For the main construction the recovery error is at least \(F\,(1-|C|/|B|)\) with \(F=1-\sqrt{2K-1}/K-\varepsilon\). For \(K=2\), \(F\approx0.134\), so the guaranteed loss is about \(0.0065(1-|C|/|B|)^2\) bits; the separate small-\(A\) constructions give \(F(2)\approx0.0156\), whose square is the \(2.4\times10^{-4}\) in the theorem.
methods.transfer: Turning an entropy deficit into a recovery problem, then bounding recovery with a well-chosen witness, works for any question of whether side information survives a channel, for example dimension bounds on extensions in squashed entanglement or in bottleneck problems.

methods.technique: An expander witness against low-rank Kraus operators
methods.explanation: Recovery after compression is a channel whose Kraus operators have small rank. A witness built from random unitaries measures how far these operators are from commuting with all of the unitaries. The expander property says no low-rank operator can come close.
math: The state is \[\rho_{AB}=\frac{1}{2K|B|}\sum_{j=1}^K\Bigl[(\ket{2j-1}\!\bra{2j-1}+\ket{2j}\!\bra{2j})\otimes I+\ket{2j-1}\!\bra{2j}\otimes U_j+\ket{2j}\!\bra{2j-1}\otimes U_j^\dagger\Bigr].\] Take \(H=\sum_j(\ket{2j-1}\!\bra{2j}\otimes U_j+\mathrm{h.c.})\). Then \(H^2\) is a projector, so \(\|H\|_\infty=1\), and Hölder's inequality gives \(\|\rho-\Phi(\rho)\|_1\ge\mathrm{Tr}[H(\rho-\Phi(\rho))]\) for \(\Phi=\mathrm{id}\otimes R\circ T\).

Write \(R\circ T=\sum_lK_l\cdot K_l^\dagger\). Expanding \(\|[K_l,U]\|_2^2\) and using \(\sum_lK_l^\dagger K_l=I\), the witness becomes \[\mathrm{Tr}[H(\rho-\Phi(\rho))]=\frac{1}{2K|B|}\sum_l\sum_{j=1}^K\bigl\|[K_l,U_j]\bigr\|_2^2.\] Hastings' theorem says the map \(X\mapsto\frac1{2K}\sum_j(U_jXU_j^\dagger+U_j^\dagger XU_j)\) has second eigenvalue near \(\sqrt{2K-1}/K\), which gives \[\frac1{2K}\sum_j\|[X,U_j]\|_2^2\ge\Bigl(1-\frac{\sqrt{2K-1}}{K}-\varepsilon\Bigr)\Bigl(\|X\|_2^2-\frac{|\mathrm{Tr}X|^2}{|B|}\Bigr).\]

Each \(K_l\) is a product of Kraus operators of \(R\) and \(T\), so its rank is at most \(|C|\), and Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(|\mathrm{Tr}K_l|^2\le|C|\,\|K_l\|_2^2\). Summing with \(\sum_l\|K_l\|_2^2=|B|\) yields the factor \(1-|C|/|B|\). Editorial check: the witness identity and the expander constants were confirmed numerically for small \(|B|\).
methods.transfer: Expander unitaries give witnesses that punish any approximately commuting low-rank structure. The same argument can bound how well a bounded quantum memory can reproduce correlations, which is relevant to locking, bounded-storage cryptography and limits on quantum learners.
